abstract.t: This specification describes several URI schemes to embed bearer tokens as authorization within URIs.

section.title: Rationale
section.t: The research on access control has shown that between the two major paradigm of access control, access control lists (ACLs) are less expressive and usually open the possibility of confused deputy attacks, which include some the most problematic attack surfaces of the Web, like XSRF. The ambient authority inherent to ACLs is also often critical in enabling privilege escalation, making one security flaw vastly more damaging.

The other paradigm, capability-based security, combines designation and permission, making it possible to prevent confused deputy attacks and create new patterns of access control, including composable security policies and safe delegation mechanisms.

HTTP/S URIs could be used as capabilities, but as HTTP/S URIs are not treated as sensitive data by most systems, except for their authorization part (which has been deprecated since), it opens up the possibility that capabilities would get leaked in various problematic places, including being stored in server logs and shown in browser address bars.
This specification describes URI schemes that make it possible to safely encode capabilities as URIs by combining a normal HTTP/S and a bearer token, called bearer-URIs.

section.title: Principle of operation
section.t: When a bearer-URI-aware HTTP agent is asked to make an HTTP request to a resource identified by a bearer-http (with parameters like the method or the request body), it MUST extract from that bearer-URI the bearer token and the HTTP URI, and prepare the HTTP request with the given parameters but put the bearer token in the Authorization header with the Bearer authorization scheme: ()
